config.title: Sliding Window Maximum

intro.title: Sliding Window Maximum
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that finds the maximum value within each sliding window of a fixed size as it moves across an array of numbers. You will learn the core concept of the sliding window algorithm, an efficient technique for processing sequential data. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays, loops, and basic conditional logic to track and compare values. By the end, you'll understand how to implement this pattern to solve lessons that involve analyzing contiguous subarrays.
intro.usecase: The sliding window maximum algorithm powers real-time data visualization in financial dashboards, where traders need to see the highest stock price over the last N minutes as charts update continuously. It's essential in network monitoring tools that display peak bandwidth usage over rolling time intervals, helping engineers identify traffic spikes. This pattern also optimizes mobile app features like fitness trackers showing your maximum heart rate during the most recent exercise segment, processing streaming sensor data efficiently.

objectives: Implement a brute force solution to find maximum values in sliding windows
Construct a deque data structure to optimize the sliding window algorithm
Manipulate array indices to maintain window boundaries during iteration
Apply the sliding window maximum algorithm to solve coding lessons
Initialize and update data structures to track candidate maximum values
Integrate edge case handling for window size validation and empty inputs
Control the deque to remove outdated indices as the window slides

content.body: Imagine you're looking through a moving camera frame at a row of numbers. You want to find the largest number visible in that frame as it slides along. That's the sliding window maximum! We'll learn how to track maximum values efficiently without recalculating everything.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Explain what a sliding window is in array lessons.
• Apply the expand-and-shrink logic to maintain window boundaries.
• Implement an algorithm to find maximum values in each window.
• Recognize when sliding window patterns apply to other lessons.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Look at this array: [3, 1, 5, 2, 4]. Imagine a window that shows only 3 numbers at a time. Starting at the beginning, the window shows [3, 1, 5]. What's the maximum in this first window?
content.title: Try it

content.body: Now slide the window one position to the right. It now shows [1, 5, 2]. What's the maximum in this second window?
content.title: Slide it

content.body: Slide once more to the right. The window shows [5, 2, 4]. What's the maximum in this third window? Notice how the window moves one step at a time, always showing exactly 3 numbers.
content.title: One more slide

content.body: You manually tracked a moving segment of the array and found the maximum in each position. For small windows, this is manageable, but what if we need to do this for thousands of numbers?
content.title: What you did

content.body: When arrays get large (like 10,000 numbers with windows of size 100), recalculating the maximum from scratch for each window becomes very slow. We need a smarter way to track the maximum as the window slides.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Think in terms of a moving segment: when to expand the window, when to shrink it. The window is like a highlight that moves across the array. We expand when we include new elements, and shrink when elements leave the window. The challenge is maintaining the maximum efficiently during these moves.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Highlight a moving segment of the array; show expand and shrink.

content.body: Instead of scanning each window completely, we'll use a data structure (like a deque) that helps us track potential maximum candidates. As the window slides, we add new elements while removing elements that are no longer in the window. This way, we always know the current maximum in constant time.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Initialize an empty deque to store indices of array elements.
2. Process the first window separately to populate the deque with relevant indices.
3. For each new element as we slide:
   • Remove indices from the back if their values are smaller than the new element.
   • Add the new element's index to the deque.
   • Remove indices from the front if they're outside the current window.
   • The front of the deque always has the maximum for the current window.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called maxSlidingWindow that takes an array nums and window size k. Return an empty array for now.
steps.hint: Remember function syntax: function maxSlidingWindow(nums, k) { ... }
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you include both parameters: nums and k.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function that accepts the array and window size.

steps.title: Handle edge cases
steps.instruction: Add an early return: if nums is empty or k is 0, return an empty array.
steps.hint: Check if nums.length is 0 or k is 0, then return [].
steps.expectedOutcome: Edge case handling at function start
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Check both conditions: empty array and zero window size.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to check if there's no data to process.

steps.title: Initialize data structures
steps.instruction: Create two arrays: result to store maximums, and deque to store indices (use an array for deque simulation).
steps.expectedOutcome: Arrays initialized for results and deque
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. We need both result and deque arrays.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need containers to store our results and window indices.

steps.title: Process the first window
steps.instruction: Loop through the first k elements. While deque isn't empty and the current element is greater than the element at the back of deque, remove from back.
steps.hint: Use a for loop for i from 0 to k-1. Compare nums[i] with nums[deque[deque.length-1]].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Well done! The deque now has indices of potential maximums.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your while condition and make sure to add the index.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to populate the deque with indices from the first window.

steps.title: add current index to deque
steps.hint: Use a for loop for i from 0 to k-1. Compare nums[i] with nums[deque[deque.length-1]].
steps.feedbackPartial: Review the instruction and try again.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Slide through remaining elements
steps.instruction: Now loop from i = k to end. First, add the front of deque to result.
steps.hint: Remember: front of deque has the maximum. Check if it's still in window range.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check all three operations: add to result, remove out-of-window, maintain decreasing order.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to handle the sliding: track maximum, remove old indices, add new ones.

steps.title: while deque isn't empty and front index is ou
steps.instruction: while deque isn't empty and front index is out of window (i - deque[0] >= k), remove from front.
steps.hint: Remember: front of deque has the maximum. Check if it's still in window range.
steps.feedbackPartial: Review the instruction and try again.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction and try again.

steps.title: while deque isn't empty and current element >
steps.instruction: while deque isn't empty and current element > back element, remove from back. Finally add current index.
steps.hint: Remember: front of deque has the maximum. Check if it's still in window range.
steps.feedbackPartial: Review the instruction and try again.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Add final maximum and return
steps.instruction: After the loop, add the front of deque to result one last time, then return result.
steps.hint: The last window's maximum is still at deque[0].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Don't forget to add the last window's maximum before returning.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to include the final window's result before returning.

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented the sliding window maximum algorithm. Remember: the window expands as we include new elements and shrinks as old elements leave. The deque helps us track potential maximums efficiently. This pattern appears in many lessons where you need to track something about a contiguous subarray as it moves through the data.
